qrdBas-a11250-d1e101.summary: Rubric for the fifth prologue question of Book 1.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e108.summary: States the question: whether theology is a science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e121.summary: First argument for the affirmative: as natural light relates to natural things, so the supernatural light of faith to supernatural things; in natural light there is science of naturals, so in the light of faith there is science of supernaturals, which is theology.
claims: Faith's light yields science of supernaturals as natural light does of naturals.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e141.summary: Second argument, by elimination among cognitive habits: theology is not faith (Augustine: many believers lack this science), opinion (it is certain), prudence, art, or understanding; so it is wisdom or science, and wisdom is a kind of science.
claims: Theology is not faith, opinion, prudence, art, or understanding, so it is science or wisdom.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e173.summary: Third argument: knowledge resting on the authority of one who cannot deceive or be deceived is no less science than knowledge resting on fallible human experience; theology rests on God's authority, whose infallibility is known even by natural reason.
claims: Knowledge based on infallible divine authority is no less science than empirical knowledge.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e193.summary: Fourth argument: if theology is not science, the theologian is not a knower, which demeans theology and theologians and makes their labour vain. Augustine's Retractationes is cited for the opposite.
claims: Denying theology is science demeans theologians.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e202.summary: Against: Augustine (Retractationes I.14) says divine science is most blessed and belongs to the beatitude of heaven, so wayfarers do not have science of divine things.
claims: Science of divine things belongs to heavenly beatitude.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e213.summary: Further: Paul (2 Cor 5) says we walk by faith, not sight, and the gloss says only by faith, so not by science.
claims: Wayfarers proceed only by faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e222.summary: Third: opined principles yield only opinion, so believed principles yield only faith, and theology's principles are believed articles of faith. The paragraph closes by announcing the procedure.
claims: Believed principles yield only faith, not science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e233.summary: First step of the plan: set out two opinions and argue against them.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e241.summary: Second step: set out the ratio of true science and its per se and accidental conditions.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e250.summary: Fourth step: respond to the reasons of the opinions.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e255.summary: Fifth step: respond to the principal arguments. The paragraph's last words begin the first opinion.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e260.summary: First opinion (Aquinas): theology is truly a science, subalternate to the science of the blessed, proceeding from principles known in the light of the higher science, namely the articles of faith, as optics is a science though it takes its principles from geometry; this is the nature of a subalternate science.
claims: Theology is a true science subalternate to the science of the blessed.
Its principles are known in the light of the higher science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e282.summary: Some illustrate with an inexperienced physician who teaches medicine from universal principles he believes on the authority of Galen or Hippocrates; he is called a knower though he only believes his principles.
claims: One can have science while only believing one's principles.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e309.summary: First argument for the opinion: a subalternate science as such is truly a science, else it would be badly distinguished from the subalternating science within the genus of science; yet it presupposes its principles from another science and has only faith of them; so likewise theology.
claims: A subalternate science is a true science though it believes its principles.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e322.summary: Second: the student of optics as such knows, and one could have optics without geometry, at least by divine power, since they are essentially distinct habits; so one can have theology as true science without the science of the blessed or evidence of its principles.
claims: One could have a subalternate science without the subalternating one.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e340.summary: Third: Aristotle and the Commentator (Ethics VI) hold that principles known by some induction suffice for science, without total evidence from terms, else sciences would have no proper principles. Principles accepted from the testimony of many trustworthy witnesses, confirmed by their lives and miracles, signs as rational as natural sensibles from which one induces, suffice no less, as in theology.
claims: Principles known by induction suffice for science.
Principles accepted from trustworthy witnesses attested by miracles suffice no less.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e371.summary: Fourth: if theology is not science because its principles are never understood but only believed, this is false; Augustine (83 Questions q.48) says some things are first believed and later understood, by the pure of heart who keep the precepts of good living.
claims: Some divine truths first believed are later understood by the pure of heart.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e391.summary: Authorities for the opinion: Augustine attributes 'this science' to theology, and Paul (1 Cor 12) distinguishes the gift of knowledge from the gift of faith, which seems to be theology.
claims: Scripture and Augustine distinguish theological science from faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e402.summary: Some, to explain this subalternation, distinguish three modes: by subject (optics to geometry), by end (bridle-making to horsemanship), and by mode of knowing the same thing more or less perfectly (navigation to astronomy regarding storms: the sailor by signs and experience, the astronomer through celestial causes). Our theology is subalternate to the blessed's science in the third mode, knowing by belief imperfectly what they know by sight perfectly.
claims: Subalternation can be by subject, by end, or by mode of knowing.
Our theology is subalternate to the blessed's science by mode of knowing.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e442.summary: Against the opinion: by its proponent's own words (Summa II-II q.1), true science does not coexist with faith about the same object, but theology does coexist with faith, so it is not truly science. Some reply that only demonstrative propter quid science, evident from self-evident principles resolved into sense-known terms, excludes faith, and that is subalternating, not subalternate, science.
claims: On Aquinas's own principles, true science cannot coexist with faith, yet theology does.
Some say only subalternating science excludes faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e477.summary: Against that reply: first, propter quid science can coexist with faith, as shown before. Second, it does not answer the argument: if science excludes faith because science is evident and faith inevident, then just as inevidence belongs to faith's ratio, evidence (of principles and object, not merely of inference) belongs to science's. So either theology is not truly science, or it does not coexist with faith, which is plainly false.
claims: If inevidence is essential to faith, evidence of principles is essential to science.
Theology cannot be both true science and compatible with faith on Aquinas's view.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e512.summary: Second argument: subalternating and subalternate sciences never concern the same truths, as induction shows even in the third mode (astronomy has prior truths, and its conclusions are the principles of the subalternate). Our theology and the blessed's concern the same truths equally first, though not equally perfectly, having the same first subject under the same ratio; covering fewer truths does not make subalternation, else knowing four geometric conclusions would be subalternate to knowing ten.
claims: Subalternating and subalternate sciences never share the same truths.
Our theology and the blessed's concern the same truths equally first.
Knowing fewer truths does not constitute subalternation.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e560.summary: Third: one with a subalternate science can simultaneously have the subalternating science and know its principles evidently, but on their view one cannot have our theology together with the blessed's science, since our theology coexists with faith and vision does not, and our knowledge is enigmatic and vision clear.
claims: A subalternate science is compatible with its subalternating science.
On their own view, our theology is incompatible with the blessed's science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e584.summary: Fourth: theology's principles cannot be evident to its possessor by resolution to sense-known terms, by induction sufficient for science, or by a higher science on which it depends (as object, principle, power, habit, species, or medium), since our theology cannot coexist with the blessed's. Calling it science is like saying one knows geometry because one believes another knows it. Science requires some evidence; theology's principles are not known from terms, and the induction the Commentator means (from many singulars to a universal) cannot yield articles like the Trinity or Incarnation, which concern a singular, God, nor can experience. So theology is not properly subalternate to the blessed's science. The paragraph ends by introducing the second opinion.
claims: Theology's principles are not evident by terms, induction, or dependence on a higher science.
Believing that another knows is not knowing.
Articles of faith about the singular God cannot be reached by induction.
Theology is not properly subalternate to the blessed's science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e660.summary: Second opinion (Henry of Ghent): our theology is, or can be, a science in a special light intermediate between the light of glory and the light of faith, in which the credibles are understood and theological conclusions deduced from them evidently and scientifically.
claims: Theology is science in a light intermediate between faith and glory.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e674.summary: They posit three grades of knowing divine things: believing (simple faithful), understanding (illuminated theologians and doctors, presupposing faith, per Isaiah 7, 'unless you believe you will not understand', and compatible with faith however scientific), and seeing (the blessed, clearly, incompatible with faith).
claims: Knowledge of God has three grades: believing, understanding, seeing.
Theological understanding coexists with faith; vision does not.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e696.summary: In that light, they say, theological terms are known evidently enough for evident principles and scientific deduction, more clearly than in natural light. Example of the eclipse: believing an astronomer, an astronomer understanding the demonstration in absence of the eclipse, and one seeing the eclipse.
claims: In the intermediate light theological terms are known clearly enough for science.
The eclipse example illustrates believing, understanding, and seeing.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e718.summary: Elsewhere they seem to say the terms are not known otherwise than in natural light, yet the complexes, principles, and deductions are evident. Argument for possibility: what God can do through an efficient cause he can do immediately; he can cause knowledge of complexes through knowledge of terms, so without it. The evidence of a complex need not come from its terms. Such light is possible, like the prophetic light in which prophets knew divine and future contingent things, neither in faith, glory, nor nature, so in an intermediate light.
claims: Evidence of a complex need not come from evidence of its terms.
God can cause evident knowledge of complexes immediately.
Prophetic light shows an intermediate light is possible.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e764.summary: They prove theology is science in such a light. Augustine (De trinitate XIV): many believers lack this science, so it is not in faith's light, else all believers would have it. Augustine on John 1 ('the life was the light of men'): the mountains receive peace (wisdom) and hills justice (faith), so the greater have wisdom beyond faith. Augustine (Contra epistolam fundamenti): through faith I hope to reach understanding, God illuminating within. Richard of St Victor (De trinitate I) seeks necessary reasons, and Anselm says his Monologion proves by necessary reasons what faith holds of the divine nature and persons.
claims: Augustine distinguishes theological science from faith possessed by many.
Richard and Anselm seek necessary reasons for articles of faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e829.summary: Further reasons: we can know any article is possible, since we know no impossibility follows from it. Any syllogism purporting to derive an impossibility errs in matter (a false premise, traceable to a first falsehood immediately recognizable, else the intellect would naturally err) or in form (detectable by the art of Sophistical Refutations). So we know no credible is impossible, hence that the articles are possible, and in eternal things possibility and being do not differ, so necessary articles are known true.
claims: We can know that no article of faith implies an impossibility.
In eternal things possibility entails actuality, so necessary articles can be known true.
concepts: in perpetuis esse et posse non differunt

qrdBas-a11250-d1e881.summary: Further: in that light, indeed even in natural light (as argued in q2, though not on their view), one can know the terms of any necessary complex, hence complexes mediate and immediate, hence science. They say this light is not infused at baptism but after long study, presupposing faith, given to those who dispose themselves. Against Henry: in his Summa he says no special light beyond faith is needed to understand the credibles, so still less to understand Scripture's literal sense and deduce conclusions; so no such light is required.
claims: The intermediate light is acquired after long study, not given at baptism.
Henry elsewhere denies any special light beyond faith is needed.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e921.summary: Others' arguments against the light: we cannot have the noblest habits hidden from us, yet no one knows or experiences such a light in himself.
claims: Noble habits cannot be hidden, yet no one experiences this light.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e934.summary: Further: the light is not sanctifying grace, since many sinners have better theology than many just; nor a gratuitous grace among the Spirit's gifts (1 Cor 12), since those are for the Church's benefit and these theologians cannot teach it; nor the gifts of Isaiah 11, which exist only with grace. And God provides at baptism all things necessary for the knowledge of faith, but not this light.
claims: The light is neither sanctifying nor gratuitous grace.
God provides at baptism what faith needs, and this light is not among it.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e971.summary: Second set of arguments, that theology cannot be true science in such a light: every believer assents to theological truths more because of the speaker's authority than because of reasoning, so has no science; and such light and science would exclude faith by their evidence.
claims: Believers assent to theological truths chiefly on authority.
Evident science would exclude faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e989.summary: Third: no one can teach theology scientifically, so no one has science of it, since the sign of the knower is the ability to teach.
claims: Theology cannot be taught scientifically.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e996.summary: Fourth: double contradictions are as incompossible as single; on their view science and opinion cannot coexist, contradicting as certain and uncertain, evident and inevident; so faith and science do not coexist, being evident and inevident; we have faith, so not science.
claims: Faith and science contradict as evident and inevident.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1012.summary: Fifth: faith is not done away with except in heaven, so here we would have faith and that science together, and by parity science and belief of the same geometric conclusion, which is false.
claims: Faith and science of the same conclusion cannot coexist.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1026.summary: Sixth: a philosopher who knows that God exists, if converted and given faith, would no longer have science of it, given the repugnance of habits; so a believer who acquired such science would lose faith.
claims: Faith and science of the same object exclude each other.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1042.summary: The author judges these arguments against the light worthless in themselves; he will resolve them and then bring other arguments against the opinion.
claims: The common objections to the intermediate light fail.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1049.summary: Reply to the first: by that reasoning no one has charity, since everyone's charity is hidden from him. The principle holds of naturally acquired habits, not infused ones, and the light would be infused.
claims: Infused habits can be hidden from their possessor.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1060.summary: Reply to the second: it could be a gratuitous grace, not sanctifying, existing without grace. It is for the Church's benefit as well as the subject's, as Dionysius says Hierotheus learned divine things by experience. Many prophets, apostles, and disciples had it. A doctor with it could teach scientifically only a disciple with the same light, or not every gratuitous grace is for the community. As a teacher of natural things needs pupils with natural light, one with this light can still exhort and persuade those without it.
claims: The light could be a gratuitous grace for the Church's benefit.
Scientific teaching in this light requires a pupil with the same light.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1112.summary: Reply to the third: at baptism God provides what is simply necessary for salvation (faith, charity), and this light is not. Against the arguments on science: the major is false. One with such science would not adhere more firmly than by faith, since nothing is more certain than one's faith, in certainty of adherence, not of evidence; he adheres in more ways but not more intensely. Or, conceding the major, whoever has the light adheres more through science, since adherence following evidence in that light exceeds adherence following testimony.
claims: Baptism provides only what is simply necessary for salvation.
Faith has supreme certainty of adherence, though not of evidence.
Adherence through faith and science together is extensively, not intensively, greater.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1149.summary: If some adhere no more than by faith, they do not have that light or science.
claims: Lack of greater adherence indicates lack of the light.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1155.summary: Reply to the second argument on science: it works ad hominem against someone denying that faith and science coexist, as the fourth argument confirms, but not against whoever posits the light while holding, as the author does, that faith and science coexist well.
claims: The argument works only against those denying the compatibility of faith and science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1171.summary: Reply to the third: one with such light can teach only a disciple disposed by the same light.
claims: Scientific teaching of theology requires a similarly illuminated pupil.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1178.summary: Reply to the fourth argument against the light: it concludes against the opinion's proponent, since one contradiction is as impossible as a hundred thousand; if opinion and science cannot coexist because of a double contradiction, neither can faith and science because of a single one. It does not touch those who hold, as the author does, that opinion, science, and faith of the same object coexist.
claims: One contradiction is as impossible as many.
Opinion, science, and faith of the same object can coexist.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1198.summary: Reply to the sixth: it tells against the proponent. The light does not necessarily presuppose faith nor conversely; each can absolutely be had without the other, though in fact the light is had only with faith accompanying or preceding.
claims: The intermediate light and faith are absolutely separable.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1211.summary: A seventh argument: every knower reflecting can know that he knows, but no one experiences knowing divine things. Reply: those with the light knew that they knew. Knowing and knowing that one knows are essentially distinct acts, the direct and the reflex, and one can occur without the other, as one often considers a conclusion without thinking about oneself. Alternatively, reflexive knowledge is guaranteed only for naturally acquired habits, not infused ones, as one cannot know that one loves God by infused charity or believes by infused faith. The second answer fits better with the first reply above.
claims: Direct and reflex knowing are distinct acts; one can occur without the other.
One cannot know reflexively that one has infused charity or faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1279.summary: The author's own assessment of the second opinion: first, such a light is not impossible, any more than the prophetic light, since he sees no repugnance on the side of subject, agent, effect, or the wayfarer state.
claims: An intermediate light is possible, like the prophetic light.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1292.summary: Second, in such a light a wayfarer can have evident knowledge and science of credibles, since theological terms can be understood well enough for evident knowledge and scientific deduction from immediate complexes, short of vision. But it is a real doubt whether complexes can be evidently known without knowing their terms otherwise than now. This seems impossible, since nothing is known without its intrinsic parts being known in the same way (a house without its parts), and terms are intrinsic parts of a proposition (Metaphysics V).
claims: In such a light, evident theological science is possible for a wayfarer.
It is doubtful that a proposition can be evident without its terms being better known.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1338.summary: Further: a complex involves a relation of extreme to extreme, and a relation is known only through its known foundation; a conclusion is known only through known premises, so still less a proposition without known terms. Against the claim that knowledge of terms is an efficient cause of knowledge of propositions, one might say it is more like matter or parts, or like knowledge of foundations relative to knowledge of relations, so it is impossible by any power to know the complex while ignoring the terms. The author leaves this in doubt.
claims: A complex, as a relation of terms, is known only through its known terms.
Knowledge of terms may be a material part of propositional knowledge, not its efficient cause.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1393.summary: Note: there are two cognitions of terms, one separately (prior at least by nature to forming the proposition) and one within the proposition. The separate cognitions can be called efficient causes of the propositional cognition, in which the terms are known indistinctly with the proposition. Naturally the first cognitions must remain, else the complex could be formed before them. They are not parts of the third, propositional cognition; by divine power it could perhaps be had without them, but the terms would still be understood by the same intellection as the complex.
claims: Separate cognitions of terms efficiently cause propositional cognition.
Within the proposition, terms are known by the same act as the complex.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1441.summary: Third, the light alone does not suffice for evident knowledge of theological terms or complexes. A light is that in or under which something is seen, neither the object nor the power, so the object must also be sufficiently present. For abstractive knowledge presence in itself is accidental, so the object must be present in a representative; but light does not represent, any more than the agent intellect's light, whereas species do, and they do not grant an impressed species, nor does God have a distinct expressed species in the phantasm. So the light gives no sufficient presence of the object.
claims: A light is neither object nor power and does not represent its object.
Evident abstractive knowledge requires the object present in a representative species.
The intermediate light alone cannot supply such presence.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1491.summary: Fourth: even granting some evident theology possible in that light with other requisites, our theology, acquired by study aided by faith, cannot be evident science, nor anything of the same kind. Here he contradicts the opinion, which seems to say the same habit acquired by faith-aided study, inevident, becomes evident science when the infused light supervenes. The same objects may be evident through another possible theology, but the same habit that was inevident can never become evident, as will be shown. Ends the first article.
claims: The same habit cannot change from inevident to evident.
Our study-acquired theology cannot become evident science by a supervening light.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1534.summary: Second article: what propter quid science properly is (Posterior Analytics I). Science formally is certain and evident intellectual cognition of a true, necessary complex evidently deduced from necessary truths previously known evidently, mediately or immediately. Each element is explained: cognition (excludes will), intellectual (excludes sense), certain (excludes suspicion and opinion, though opinion is not repugnant to certainty), evident by its own testimony (excludes faith, which rests on another's testimony), true (excludes error), necessary (excludes contingents and corruptible singulars), complex (excludes simple understanding of terms), evidently deduced (excludes paralogism), from necessary truths (excludes false-graphic and dialectical syllogism), previously known (excludes understanding of immediate principles, priority by nature sufficing), and mediately or immediately (includes subalternate sciences).
claims: Science is certain, evident cognition of a necessary complex deduced evidently from necessary truths known evidently.
Faith differs from science by resting on another's testimony.
Science is of necessary truths only, not corruptible singulars.
Priority of principles by nature suffices.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1669.summary: These are per se conditions of science, taken not broadly to include faith (as Augustine, De trinitate XV: far be it from us to deny we know what we learn by testimony), nor as distinguished from wisdom (Augustine, De trinitate XII: wisdom of eternal, science of human things), but as Aristotle takes it (Posterior Analytics I): knowing the cause through which a thing is, that it is its cause, and that it cannot be otherwise, by demonstration from true, first, immediate, better known, and prior premises. This holds of science both as habit and as act.
claims: Science is taken in the strict Aristotelian sense, not Augustine's broader senses.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1721.summary: Some conditions belong to sciences not as sciences absolutely but because they concern created objects, or exist in certain intellects, or for other reasons.
claims: Some conditions of science are accidental, deriving from created objects or knowers.
concepts: per se and accidental conditions of science

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1739.summary: First accidental condition, from the object: science is of universals. If this were per se, there could be no science of any singular, including God. Every science of creatures is of universals, since science concludes a proper attribute of an adequate subject, and no created singular determines a proper attribute to itself (Socrates cannot determine risibility to himself rather than Plato), whereas the species does.
claims: Universality of science's object is accidental, deriving from created objects.
No created singular determines a proper attribute to itself.
Science of the singular God is possible.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1789.summary: Second: science is acquired through a demonstrative middle that is a definition, since every created species is limited to a genus and difference, or matter and form, from which propter quid demonstration proceeds. This is not needed for the unlimited singular God, who need not have intrinsic principles, be a species, or be universal, yet there can be propter quid science of him.
claims: Definitional middle terms are needed only for created objects.
There can be propter quid science of God without definition or intrinsic principles.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1826.summary: Third: no science concludes that an attribute essentially distinct from its subject actually inheres in it, since the conclusion would be falsifiable, as God can make any essentially prior thing without the posterior.
claims: Science cannot conclude the actual inherence of a really distinct attribute.
God can separate any prior from its posterior.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1853.summary: Fourth: science proceeds from causes of the subject or of the attribute's inherence, because created objects are caused. This does not hold universally, as of God, who cannot be caused; yet about God immediate complexes can be formed from which others are demonstrated propter quid and a priori, as if they were really distinct and caused.
claims: Proceeding from causes is accidental to science, deriving from created objects.
Propter quid demonstration about God proceeds from quasi-prior complexes.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1892.summary: Fifth: from the imperfection of the subject, science proceeds by syllogistic discourse in which principles are known before conclusions in nature and time, due to the intellect's potentiality. In the perfect divine intellect, always in act, there is no real discourse; by one simple intuition it knows terms, principles, and conclusions in an order of reason only. Likewise science in a creature is created, but not in God, where it is rather a cause. Ends the second article.
claims: Discursive reasoning is accidental to science, arising from the intellect's potentiality.
God knows all by one simple intuition in an order of reason only.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1938.summary: Third article: whether theology is science properly. Theology is threefold: God's, the blessed's, and wayfarers'; each concerns necessary and contingent truths.
claims: Theology divides into God's, the blessed's, and wayfarers', each of necessary and contingent truths.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e1956.summary: God's theology concerning secondary, mediate necessary complexes is most truly science formally, since all per se conditions hold. Where several perfections are ordered to a first and contained in it, one can be demonstrated of the first through it, or a third of the first through the second. Against those who say no second perfection can be demonstrated propter quid of the utterly simple first, the perfections in God are essentially ordered as if really distinct, however distinguished, since infinite regress is impossible.
claims: God's theology of mediate necessary truths is science in the strictest sense.
Divine perfections are essentially ordered and so permit propter quid demonstration.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2004.summary: God's theology of contingents is certain, evident, and infallible, but not properly science, lacking the condition of necessity, though it has some conditions of knowing.
claims: God's knowledge of contingents is certain and evident but not science properly.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2015.summary: The blessed's theology is twofold. Their theology of mediate, complex necessary truths is truly propter quid science, though they have one simple intuition of all in the Word, which by natural order falls on terms, then principles, then conclusions. In God and the blessed, knowing the principle is not the ratio of knowing the conclusion; the divine essence is the ratio of knowing them all in order, as if one were known from the other, which illuminates the earlier definition of science.
claims: The blessed's theology of necessary truths is true propter quid science.
In God and the blessed the divine essence, not the principle, is the ratio of knowing the conclusion.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2075.summary: The blessed's theology of contingents is not properly science, lacking a necessary object, though it is certain and evident through the first theological object. It resembles understanding of principles, at least for the first contingent truth, if indeed the blessed know any contingents in the Word, which is doubtful, since it does not take its principle from a prior complex.
claims: The blessed's knowledge of contingents is certain but not science.
It resembles understanding of first principles.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2104.summary: Wayfarers' theology: one kind, possible abstractive evident demonstrative theology of mediate necessary truths about God (q1), is most truly science, whether or not it is had in the intermediate light; a wayfarer with nothing incompatible with that state can truly know by it.
claims: Evident abstractive theology possible to a wayfarer is science in the strict sense.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2128.summary: Theology of contingents possible to a wayfarer by abstractive and evident revelation is not science properly, like the other theologies of contingents.
claims: Revealed evident knowledge of contingents is not science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2139.summary: The other wayfarers' theology is what doctors now have, trained in Scripture, aided by faith and natural light, by which they expound Scripture, resolve controversies, nourish faith in Catholics, defend it against heretics, clarify doubts, and argue for purely theological truths, as modern theologians do. It has two parts. The part about contingent articles (the Word incarnate and what follows) is not science properly, since its object is contingent.
claims: Our theology serves to expound Scripture, resolve controversies, and defend faith.
Our theology of contingent articles is not science, lacking a necessary object.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2181.summary: Our theology of necessary, purely theological truths, and what follows necessarily from them, is not and cannot be science properly, remaining the same in species or number. It is neither subalternating nor subalternate, and not science in the light of faith, nature, the intermediate light, or glory, were it possible there.
claims: Our theology of necessary truths is not and cannot be science properly.
It is not science in any light, nor subalternate.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2201.summary: First argument that our theology is not science: a habit that does not make its possessor truly know, in whatever light, is not science, as whiteness always makes its subject white. This theology inheres in many theologians without making them evidently knowing, since every holder assents more because of the speaker's authority than because of any deduction.
claims: A habit that does not make its possessor know is not science.
Theologians assent to theological truths chiefly on authority.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2239.summary: Second: the conclusion cannot be more certain than the principle (Posterior Analytics I), and in purely theological reasoning the principle is only believed, assented to on authority or Scripture's testimony; so no conclusion is ever known through this habit.
claims: A conclusion cannot exceed its principles in certainty.
Theology's principles are only believed.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2257.summary: Third: the act and habit of science depend only on object, power, principles, and the light, not on the will's assent (the will only joins the intellect's gaze to the object). This theological habit necessarily depends on the will's assent to matters of faith, on all views, since all presuppose faith, and no one believes except willingly; so it is not scientific.
claims: Scientific assent does not depend on the will; theological assent does.
No one believes except willingly.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2290.summary: Further: by the same reasoning any opinion about necessary things could become science in a higher light or by divine power, which is impossible, as faith or opinion cannot be science. If God caused the same knowledge immediately without the will, it would not change its nature, as an opinion caused immediately without its probable middle is still opinion, and a created man is of the same kind as a generated one.
claims: Changing the cause of a cognition does not change its nature.
Opinion and faith cannot become science in any light.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2325.summary: Further: theology would be science either from certainty of adherence to its premises (then faith would be science), from evidence of inference (which holds even among falsehoods, as 'an ass is a man, so an ass is risible'), or from a supervening light (which does not change its nature).
claims: Neither certainty of adherence, nor validity of inference, nor a supervening light makes theology science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2347.summary: Further, to the proponent of the light: when the light supervenes, does this theology remain in its nature (then it is not science, as before), is it corrupted (then it is nothing), or is it transformed into another (of the same kind, then not science; of another kind, then nothing of this kind is science, which is the point)? 'Perfected' would require addition of the same kind, not changing its species.
claims: A habit cannot become science by a supervening light without ceasing to be the same habit.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2389.summary: Conclusion: our theology is not and cannot be proper science, as a man cannot be an ass. In essentially ordered things, if the first fails, the second fails; evidence of principle and conclusion are essentially ordered in scientific procedure, so without evidence in the principle there is none in the conclusion.
claims: Our theology cannot be science in principle.
Lack of evidence in principles entails lack of evidence in conclusions.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2412.summary: What habit then do theologians have beyond simple believers? A habit of declaring Scripture, arguing from it, and resolving apparent contradictions, from its own resources (expounding one passage by another) or from other sciences (showing possibility). None of these, as theological, is scientific or evident. Arguing from one passage to another, both are believed. Paul's 'if Christ rose, we shall rise' is no demonstration, since both are believed. When philosophy is mixed into theology, any evidence comes from the alien science, yielding only probability about purely theological matters; and mixed with believed premises, the conclusion follows the weaker premise.
claims: Theologians have a habit of expounding and harmonizing Scripture, not scientific evidence.
Scriptural arguments in purely theological matters are not demonstrations.
Philosophical arguments give only probability in purely theological matters.
The conclusion follows the weaker premise.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2490.summary: So the pure theologian as such has no evident habit that can properly be called science, only science in Augustine's broad sense of what we learn by testimony: an explicative, declarative, harmonizing habit about Scripture acquired by study with natural light aided by faith, which can be called a 'certain extended faith' (fides quaedam extensa). Ends the third article.
claims: The theologian's habit is science only in a broad sense.
Theology is a kind of extended faith acquired by study.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2514.summary: Note: believers commonly have infused faith in the articles and also acquired faith in what Scripture proposes to be believed; theologians have the same.
claims: Believers and theologians have both infused and acquired faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2530.summary: Second, theologians have a habit of declaring, expounding, and harmonizing Scripture from its own resources. This can be called theology in some way, while the first habit is rather called faith, though also theological in some way.
claims: The exegetical habit can in some way be called theology.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2548.summary: Third, a habit of deducing theological conclusions from the articles and believed truths as principles. This is more properly called theology, being more like the scientific mode of other sciences; it is what is commonly acquired by study.
claims: The deductive habit from articles is theology most properly as commonly had.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2568.summary: Fourth, a habit of defending or proving by philosophers' demonstrative or probable reasons used in service of theology, which is philosophy rather than theology, unless the defense is from theology's own resources, which belongs to the second and third habits. All these can be acquired naturally (except infused faith) or by intellect aided by faith. A fifth, abstractive theology possible to a wayfarer (q1), is not commonly had or naturally acquirable. The paragraph ends by introducing the fourth article.
claims: Philosophical defense of faith is philosophy, not theology.
Theological habits besides infused faith can be naturally acquired.
Evident abstractive theology is not commonly had nor naturally acquirable.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2604.summary: Heading of the fourth article: resolving the others' reasons.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2609.summary: Reply to the first opinion's first argument: a subalternate science as such is science, but it is false that it has only faith of its principles. It has evident knowledge of them from sense (optics from the reflection of rays) or from the higher science proving them; otherwise it is not actually science. To know optics without geometry, if its principles were evident only through geometry, is to say nothing. The inexperienced physician who only believes his principles has no science. Asked why such are made masters, he retorts: why are theologians made masters, when the greatest doctors said theology is not properly science, or canonists and legists? Or medicine can be had by experience, unlike our theology.
claims: A subalternate science must have evident knowledge of its principles, by sense or the higher science.
Merely believing principles does not yield science.
Academic mastership does not imply science in the strict sense.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2679.summary: Reply to the second: optics could exist without geometry by divine power, even by nature, if its principles are knowable not only through geometry but by reduction to sense. If God could give the same evidence of its principles immediately, optics would stand without geometry; but in theology there is no evidence from God or elsewhere.
claims: Optics could exist without geometry only if its principles were evident otherwise.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2710.summary: Reply to the third: the Commentator speaks of common principles acquired by induction from sensible singulars, which does not apply to the articles of faith.
claims: Induction from sensibles does not apply to the articles of faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2723.summary: Reply to the fourth: purely theological truths are never evidently understood through our theology. Augustine's 'understanding' either means improperly the explication described, applies in heaven to the perfectly pure of heart fulfilling the precept of charity, or refers to the revealed abstractive theology possible to a wayfarer (q1), which, very probably, great 'mountains' like John had. In the other Augustine passage, 'science' is taken broadly for faith or any certain knowledge.
claims: Our theology never yields evident understanding of purely theological truths.
Augustine's 'understanding' refers to heaven, broad explication, or extraordinary revealed knowledge.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2756.summary: Reply to Paul's 'gift of knowledge': answered similarly, or Paul means the possible abstractive science that he himself seems to have had, not our theology. The paragraph closes by turning to the second opinion.
claims: Paul's gift of knowledge refers to the revealed abstractive science he had.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2768.summary: Reply to the second opinion's first authority (Augustine's 'huic scientiae tribuo'): he speaks of science broadly.
claims: Augustine uses 'science' broadly.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2777.summary: Reply to the second (the 'peace' by which the mountains are illumined): this peace is not our theology but the possible theology given to John and Paul, in the posited light or not; or if it is our theology, it is not therefore science properly.
claims: The wisdom of the 'mountains' is extraordinary revealed theology, not ours.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2790.summary: Reply to Richard: necessary reasons for many theological truths can be adduced through that other possible theology, perhaps in the light the author considers possible, or by the blessed in glory, but not through our theology; such reasons escape us.
claims: Necessary reasons for theological truths are available only to extraordinary or beatific theology.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2808.summary: Reply to Contra epistolam fundamenti: Augustine means either the true science of heaven toward which we walk by faith (as 'God illumining the mind within' suggests), or our theology, called 'true science' as the science of men, though improperly.
claims: Augustine's 'science' there means heavenly science or science improperly.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2826.summary: Reply to Anselm: he does not evidently assign demonstrations; the same answers apply to him and to similar authorities that make theology sound like science. The paragraph closes by turning to the second opinion's reasons.
claims: Anselm's 'necessary reasons' are not evident demonstrations.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2837.summary: Reply to the second opinion's reasons: in such a light, by some possible evident theology, or perhaps even without the light, purely theological truths could be known demonstratively, but never through our theology, whatever light supervenes. Against 'we know possible whatever implies no impossibility': the last impossible implies no further impossible yet is not known possible, and a first impossibility may imply nothing more evidently impossible. Against the minor, we merely believe the articles are not impossible. Against detecting formal fallacies by the art of Sophistical Refutations: knowing the art in general does not mean applying it in every matter; Aristotle himself could not have solved a tenth of the formally fallacious arguments that could be made, and would have been tied up 'like a goat'.
claims: We do not know the articles are possible; we believe it.
Lack of a derivable impossibility does not prove possibility.
Knowing logic in general does not enable detecting every fallacy.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2916.summary: Second, the syllogism can err in matter with false premises whose falsity is not evident to us. Aristotle concluded the eternity of the world from falsehoods without seeing their falsity; he did not err naturally, since he should have remained neutral, as appearances do not lead to the novelty of the world but do not lead to its eternity either. He extended appearances too far, supposing that since the heaven moves now it always did. We should remain neutral, not knowing whether the syllogism errs or concludes.
claims: False premises need not be evidently false to us.
Aristotle erred about the world's eternity by overextending appearances.
Natural reason should remain neutral on the world's eternity.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e2971.summary: Another doctor answers: we can know of any proposition against an article that it is not necessary, but we cannot prove every false contrary proposition false, so we do not know evidently that nothing impossible follows. Example: 'no one essence subsists in three persons; in the Trinity one essence would; so there is no Trinity': we can know the major is not necessary, since induction from limited created essences commits the fallacy of the consequent, but this does not tell us whether there is a Trinity. As refuting 'stars are even because incorruptible' does not tell whether they are even or odd, solving objections to articles does not make us know them.
claims: Refuting objections to the articles does not yield knowledge of them.
Induction from created essences does not apply to the divine essence.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e3039.summary: Reply to the second reason: as answered in q2 to the last argument for the philosophers' position. The paragraph closes by turning to the principal argument on supernatural light.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e3048.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: a light in which true science is had is possible, but it is not and cannot be the light of faith, which is imperfect and insufficient for understanding divine things evidently, unlike natural light for lower things; it suffices only as a light for its own act, believing.
claims: The light of faith suffices only for believing, not for science.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e3070.summary: Reply to the second: our theology is a kind of extended faith acquired by study with talent and natural light added to faith, by which one can do the works mentioned (expound, defend) that simple believers cannot. Alternatively it is science or wisdom only improperly.
claims: Our theology is an extended faith enabling exegesis and defense of faith.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e3088.summary: Reply to the third: though it can be demonstrated that God, on whose testimony Scripture rests, cannot deceive or be deceived, it is not evident but only believed that God said these things. This is evidence from another's testimony, not from the object itself, so it yields certainty of adherence, not of evidence, and is not science.
claims: God's veracity can be demonstrated, but that God revealed these truths is only believed.
Testimony gives certainty of adherence, not evidence.

qrdBas-a11250-d1e3111.summary: Reply to the last: the theologian as such is not a knower in the proper sense, but this does not demean theology, since knowing what it knows about God is nobler than knowing all lower things (Aristotle, De partibus animalium: better to know a little less certainly about higher things than much more certainly about lower). Theologians should be held in the greatest reverence.
claims: The theologian is not a knower in the strict sense, but theology is the noblest knowledge.
Little knowledge of higher things outweighs much of lower things.

qrdBas-a11250.summary: Prologue q5 asks whether theology is a science. Bassolis rejects two opinions. Against Aquinas's view that our theology is a science subalternate to the science of the blessed (like optics to geometry, or navigation to astronomy), he argues that true science would then coexist with faith, which Aquinas denies. He adds that subalternating and subalternate sciences never share the same truths, that a subalternate science must be compatible with its superior and have evident principles, and that believing another knows is not knowing. Against Henry of Ghent's view that theology is science in a light intermediate between faith and glory, he first rebuts the usual objections (infused habits can be hidden, the light could be a gratuitous grace, faith and science coexist). He grants such a light is possible, like the prophetic, but doubts that propositions can be evident without better-known terms, and argues that a light does not represent its object and that the same habit cannot change from inevident to evident. He defines science strictly: certain, evident intellectual cognition of a necessary complex evidently deduced from evidently known necessary truths. Universality, definitional middles, causes, and discursiveness are only accidental conditions arising from created objects or knowers. God's and the blessed's theology of necessary truths is science properly, as is the evident abstractive theology possible to a wayfarer; all theology of contingents is certain cognition but not science. Our theology, as doctors have it, is not and cannot be science, because its assent rests on authority and the will, its conclusions cannot exceed believed principles, and no supervening light changes the habit. It is a 'certain extended faith' comprising exegetical, harmonizing, and deductive habits, while philosophical defense of faith is philosophy. He adds that we only believe the articles are possible (refuting objections is not knowing them), and that Aristotle erred on the eternity of the world by overextending appearances. Theology nonetheless remains the noblest knowledge.
claims: Our theology is not subalternate to the science of the blessed, nor science in an intermediate light.
Science strictly is certain, evident cognition of necessary complexes deduced from evident necessary premises; universality and causal demonstration are accidental conditions.
God's and the blessed's theology of necessary truths, and possible evident abstractive theology, are sciences; knowledge of contingents is not.
Our theology is not and cannot be science, since its principles are only believed and assent depends on the will.
Our theology is a 'certain extended faith' with exegetical, harmonizing, and deductive habits.
We do not know but believe the articles are possible; refuting objections does not yield knowledge.
